title: Retrospective descriptive assessment of clinical decision support medication-related alerts in two Saudi Arabian hospitals
authors: Jamilah Ahmed Alsaidan, Jane Portlock, Sondus I. Ata, Hisham S. Aljadhey, Bryony Dean Franklin
venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making 22:101
metadata_verified_via: Full-text PDF (UCL Discovery repository); Springer link record
objective: Describe frequency, types and override of rule-based CDSS medication alerts and appropriateness of overrides
architecture_methods: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of system-generated CDSS alert reports; appropriateness review of a sample of overridden alerts against health records
models_tools: Cerner Millennium CPOE (2014 version) with rule-based CDSS (11 alert types)
dataset_sample: King Saud University Medical City, Riyadh (KKUH 850 beds, KAUH 250 beds); Jun 2015-Dec 2017; 5,114,310 orders; 4,446,730 alerts; 307 overridden alerts reviewed
metrics: Alert rate, override rate by alert type and setting, appropriateness of display and override
baselines: Comparison with rates previously reported in literature (no control)
main_findings: 4,231,743/4,446,730 alerts (95.2%) overridden; outpatient 97.8%, inpatient 93.6%; drug duplicate 79.8% of alerts (94.7% overridden), dose range 11.1% (97.8%), drug interaction 7.2% (97.3%), drug allergy 0.3% (91.3%), new drug allergy 49.3%, stop order 1.9%; 37.7% of overrides with no reason selected; of 307 sampled overrides 80.1% displayed appropriately, 79.5% overridden appropriately; lowest appropriate override for new drug allergy 43.2% and drug allergy 62.2%
limitations: Single medical city and CPOE; small appropriateness sample; record-only judgement; no specialty analysis; no patient-outcome data; accepted alerts only counted
relevance: P1/P2, RQ1: local evidence that low-specificity interruptive decision support is overwhelmingly overridden (alert fatigue), relevant to unnecessary escalation
supports_or_contradicts: Supports need for specific, well-calibrated escalation/caveat statuses; pre-LLM, says nothing about multi-agent premise
claims_supported: Saudi tertiary-care CDSS alerts are overridden at very high rates

title: ChatGPT and the Future of Digital Health: A Study on Healthcare Workers' Perceptions and Expectations
authors: Temsah MH, Aljamaan F, Malki KH, Alhasan K, Altamimi I, et al. (last: Al-Eyadhy A)
objective: Assess Saudi healthcare workers' familiarity, use, trust and expectations of ChatGPT
architecture_methods: Online cross-sectional survey, 21 Feb-6 Mar 2023; regression for trust
dataset_sample: 1,057 healthcare workers in Saudi Arabia (48.8% physicians; 31.4% interns/students)
main_findings: 18.4% had used ChatGPT for healthcare; 50.9% unfamiliar with term; 75.1% comfortable to some degree; 39.5% saw value in providing medical decisions vs 65.9% research aid; 76.7% expected positive effect; obstacles: credibility/unknown sources 46.9%, harmful/wrong recommendations 40.2%, medicolegal 30.8%, confidentiality 25.8%; trust described as moderate to low (trust regression OR 0.804, p=0.085)
limitations: Convenience/social-media sampling; half unfamiliar with tool; no regional data; ChatGPT-3.5 first three months only; self-report
relevance: Context for P2/RQ1: clinicians worried about wrong recommendations and unknown sources (P3)
supports_or_contradicts: Supports need for source-grounded, overseen CDS; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Saudi HCWs in 2023 had low ChatGPT use and limited trust in AI-generated medical decisions

title: Perceptions of large language models in medical education and clinical practice among pediatric emergency physicians in Saudi Arabia: a multiregional cross-sectional study
authors: Yara AlGoraini, Mashhour Alsayyali, Ola Alotaibi, Ibtihal Almeshawi, Fahad Alaifan, Rawan Alrashed
published_version_checked: n/a (journal article); also in PMC (PMC12343484, not read due to captcha)
objective: Assess PEM physicians' perceptions of LLMs in education and clinical practice, including rating of a ChatGPT croup response
architecture_methods: Web-based cross-sectional questionnaire with one ChatGPT-4o scenario response (April 2024); logistic regression for AI use
dataset_sample: 100 pediatric emergency physicians, five Saudi regions (Central 47%)
metrics: Self-reported percentages; ratings of one ChatGPT answer
main_findings: 96% expect major future role; 77% agreed AI could assist differential diagnosis/treatment recommendations; 59% comfortable using AI for clinical decision support; 60% thought ChatGPT medical answers generally accurate; croup response rated high validity by 85%, strong reasoning 88%; 67% believed they could answer better; 66% prefer textbooks for complex topics; concerns: accuracy 83%, patient safety 56%, ethics/legal 54%, lack of regulatory guidance 52%, privacy 34%; no significant predictors of AI use; prior use reported inconsistently (79% vs 13% never-users in Fig 1)
limitations: Cross-sectional; single specialty; one prompt/one fictional scenario; self-report; internal inconsistency in use figures
relevance: Context for RQ1 and governance: clinicians want regulation and worry about accuracy and safety
supports_or_contradicts: Supports human-oversight design; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Saudi PEM physicians see potential for LLM decision support but cite accuracy, safety and regulatory gaps

title: Understanding Physician Attitudes Toward AI in Clinical Decision-Making: Cross-Sectional Study
authors: Fahad Alhazmi
published_version_checked: n/a (journal article; JMIR preprint 79730 exists); PMC12685282
objective: Assess KSA-licensed physicians' attitudes to AI in clinical decision-making, ethics and barriers
architecture_methods: Online Qualtrics survey Feb-Apr 2025, CHERRIES, descriptive statistics only
dataset_sample: 201 complete responses of 218 physicians licensed in KSA
main_findings: 25.9% used AI in past year; 82.1% trusted AI-based recommendations in clinical decision-making (49.3% strongly); 63.7% believe AI will always require human oversight; 76.6% expect efficiency gains; 52.2% think AI could harm physician-patient relationship; 54.7% concerned about bias; 52.2% privacy; 38.8% think physicians accountable for AI errors; 85.1% patients must be told when AI involved; 97% at least one barrier
limitations: Small convenience sample; self-report; no inferential analysis; generic AI not LLMs; several mismatched citations noted in extraction
relevance: Governance/transparency context; human oversight and disclosure expectations
supports_or_contradicts: Supports physician-decides and transparency design; contradicts Temsah 2023 on trust level (different construct)
claims_supported: Saudi physicians expect human oversight and patient disclosure of AI use

title: ChatGPT Conquers the Saudi Medical Licensing Exam: Exploring the Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Medical Knowledge Assessment and Implications for Modern Medical Education
authors: Aljindan FK, Al Qurashi AA, Albalawi IAS, Alanazi AMM, Aljuhani HAM, Almutairi FF, Aldamigh OA, Halawani IR, Zino Alarki SMK
objective: Evaluate GPT-4 accuracy on SMLE-style questions
architecture_methods: 220 questions across four disciplines; analysis by difficulty and section
main_findings: Overall accuracy 88.6%; lower on Hard questions; consistent across disciplines; errors clustered in option-A items
limitations: Knowledge exam not clinical decision-making; question source/contamination unclear; abstract only; Cureus light review
relevance: P4: exam-accuracy evaluation style that Chapter 1 critiques
supports_or_contradicts: Shows high exam accuracy but does not address realistic decisions
claims_supported: GPT-4 scored 88.6% on 220 SMLE-style questions

title: Evaluating the Accuracy of Medical Information Generated by ChatGPT and Gemini and Its Alignment With International Clinical Guidelines From the Surviving Sepsis Campaign: Comparative Study
authors: Dina Kutbi, Ehab Abou-Bakr, Hassan Mousa Haidar
published_version_checked: Near-identical article also in Frontiers in Digital Health 2026 (doi per URL 10.3389/fdgth.2026.1672941, accepted 20 Jan 2026): possible duplicate publication
metadata_verified_via: JMIR publisher page; Frontiers publisher page
objective: Assess alignment of ChatGPT and Gemini answers with Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 guideline
architecture_methods: Guideline rephrased as 18 questions; blinded scoring by 7 intensivists on 3-point scale; Mann-Whitney U
main_findings: ChatGPT 5 (28%) perfect, 12 (67%) nearly perfect, 1 (5%) low quality, kappa 0.656; Gemini 3 (17%), 14 (78%), 1 (5%), kappa 0.582; U=184, P=.48; ChatGPT low-quality answer contradicted guideline on VTE prophylaxis with incorrect renal enoxaparin dose; Gemini misleading procalcitonin antibiotic answer (mean 1.1); both often omitted time frames and dosing details
limitations: 18 questions, one guideline, one date; coarse rubric; single-hospital panel; general-purpose models only; discussion wording inconsistent with results; duplicate-publication concern
relevance: P1/P3, RQ1: guideline adherence errors including dosing; static QA
supports_or_contradicts: Supports excluding dosing and verifying against guideline sources; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Chatbots mostly near-correct on sepsis guideline questions but omit timing and dosing and occasionally give wrong doses

title: Evaluating the accuracy of ChatGPT in delivering patient instructions for medications: an exploratory case study
authors: Norah Othman Abanmy, Nadia Al-Ghreimil, Jawza F. Alsabhan, Heyam Al-Baity, Rana Aljadeed
objective: Evaluate correctness, completeness, harm and adherence risk of ChatGPT patient medication instructions
architecture_methods: Five sessions per drug; Likert survey adapted from Jeblick et al.; compared to Micromedex CareNotes
dataset_sample: 3 drugs (tirzepatide, citalopram, apixaban), 15 reports; 4 pharmacy experts, 33 PharmD interns
metrics: Likert ratings of correctness, completeness, potential harm, poor adherence
main_findings: Experts judged nearly all reports incomplete; 3/4 experts judged tirzepatide and apixaban reports correct, citalopram disputed; interns more lenient (e.g., citalopram v4 100% correct); authors: not a reliable standalone source
limitations: Three drugs; simulated questions; no statistics; single model; subjective ratings; figure/methods count mismatch
relevance: P1/P3: incompleteness of drug information; patient-facing rather than physician CDS
supports_or_contradicts: Supports no-prescribing/no-dosing scope; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: ChatGPT-3.5 medication instructions judged incomplete by Saudi pharmacy experts

title: Assessment of ChatGPT-generated medical Arabic responses for patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
authors: Saleh A Alqahtani, Reem S AlAhmed, Waleed S AlOmaim, Saad Alghamdi, Waleed Al-Hamoudi, Khalid Ibrahim Bzeizi, Ali Albenmousa, Alessio Aghemo, Nicola Pugliese, Cesare Hassan, Faisal A Abaalkhail
objective: Assess accuracy, completeness and comprehensibility of ChatGPT Arabic answers to MASLD patient questions
architecture_methods: English questionnaire translated to Arabic, entered 12 Nov 2023; Likert ratings by experts; Kendall's W
dataset_sample: MASLD patient questions (number not stated in record) in 3 domains; 10 Saudi native-Arabic MASLD experts
main_findings: Accuracy 4.9+/-0.94 (nearly all correct); completeness 2.4+/-0.53; comprehensibility 2.74+/-0.52; Kendall's W mean 0.28, 0.22, 0.25 (low-moderate agreement)
limitations: Single model/date; no English comparison; low rater concordance; record-level reading only
relevance: Q2 Arabic localisation; patient-facing
supports_or_contradicts: Arabic patient answers rated mostly correct; does not test CDS
claims_supported: Saudi experts rated ChatGPT-3.5 Arabic MASLD answers nearly all correct with low agreement

title: Optimizing Large Language Models for Arabic Healthcare Communication: A Focus on Patient-Centered NLP Applications
authors: Rasheed Mohammad, Omer S. Alkhnbashi, Mohammad Hammoudeh, et al.
objective: Evaluate and fine-tune ChatGPT-3.5 for Arabic (MSA and dialect) medical Q&A
architecture_methods: Fine-tuning on Altibbi Q&A; expert ratings before/after; kappa; paired t-test
dataset_sample: About 550 Q&A pairs selected from about 100,000 Altibbi pairs; MSA plus Egyptian, Saudi, Syrian, Sudanese, Moroccan dialects; 7 specialist raters
metrics: Expert accuracy rating, kappa, Jaccard similarity, length
main_findings: Accuracy 86.55% before vs 90% after fine-tuning (95% CI 85.5-87.6 vs 89-91), kappa 0.78 to 0.85, p<0.01; Egyptian 92% vs Moroccan 85% on fever/headache queries; outputs did not reliably match user dialect; ChatGPT about 100 words vs experts about 45
limitations: Seven raters, convenience; narrow specialties; no validation loss; one-month window Oct 2023; single model
relevance: Q2 localisation: dialect and code-switching, including Saudi dialect
supports_or_contradicts: Shows dialect variation affects quality; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Dialect affects Arabic medical answer quality and dialect matching is unreliable

title: MedAraBench: Large-Scale Arabic Medical Question Answering Dataset and Benchmark
authors: Mouath Abu-Daoud, Leen Kharouf, Omar El Hajj, Dana El Samad, Mariam Al-Omari, Jihad Mallat, Khaled Saleh, Nizar Habash, Farah E. Shamout
venue: arXiv 2602.01714; listed as ICLR 2026 poster (track unconfirmed)
published_version_checked: yes - ICLR 2026 poster page exists (iclr.cc/virtual/2026/poster/10011856); main vs workshop not confirmed
objective: Build and benchmark a large Arabic medical MCQ dataset
architecture_methods: Digitised regional medical school exams; zero-shot, few-shot, QLoRA; expert and LLM-judge review
models_tools: 15-16 models incl. GPT-o3, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek-V3, Llama-3.3-70B, ALLaM-7B, Fanar, Med42-8B, Apollo-7B
main_findings: GPT-o3 0.765, GPT-5 0.764, Claude Sonnet 4 0.694, GPT-4.1 0.673, Gemini 2.0 Flash 0.654, DeepSeek-V3 0.620, Llama-3.3-70B 0.547, Fanar 0.498, Med42-8B 0.318, Apollo-7B 0.238, Llama-3.1-8B 0.170 (0.320 after QLoRA); expert kappa 0.152-0.555; LLM-as-judge weakly aligned with experts

relevance: Q2; P4: Arabic exam accuracy; weak LLM-judge alignment relevant to RQ2 evaluation methods
supports_or_contradicts: Frontier models strong, Arabic-centric and medical small models weak; neutral on multi-agent

title: Cross-Lingual Empirical Evaluation of Large Language Models for Arabic Medical Tasks
authors: Chaimae Abouzahir, Congbo Ma, Nizar Habash, Farah E. Shamout
venue: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Linguistic Analysis for Health (HeaLing 2026), ACL, pp. 158-171
metadata_verified_via: ACL Anthology; numbers from arXiv v1 HTML
objective: Diagnose Arabic vs English performance gaps of medical LLMs
architecture_methods: MedAraBench test vs Google-Translate English version; letter MCQ, free text, confidence and explanation prompting; tokenisation analysis
models_tools: DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama 3.3 70B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B, Meditron 3 70B, Med42-70B, MedGemma-27B
metrics: Accuracy; token-level sequence match; tokens per word; confidence-accuracy correlation
main_findings: Arabic/English: DeepSeek-V3.2 62.39/62.85; Llama 3.3 70B 42.10/57.61; Mistral 50.25/57.75; Meditron 50.51/58.80; Med42-70B 33.59/53.21 (gap 19.62); MedGemma 49.22/52.30; Arabic about 2.4 tokens/word vs 1.5-1.6; confidence-accuracy correlation reported r=-0.56 Ar, -0.50 En (definition not checked); explanation prompting dropped DeepSeek English from 62.85 to 45.85
limitations: One language pair; English prompts for Arabic items; unvalidated machine translation; 4-bit 70B models; table inconsistency for Meditron
relevance: Q2; P1/P2, RQ3: language as robustness axis; confidence unreliable
supports_or_contradicts: Supports not relying on LLM self-confidence for abstention; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Arabic-English gap varies by model; self-confidence weak indicator

title: Benchmarking the Medical Understanding and Reasoning of Large Language Models in Arabic Healthcare Tasks
authors: Nouar AlDahoul, Yasir Zaki
objective: Benchmark LLMs on Arabic medical MCQ and open-ended tasks
architecture_methods: Prompt variants; majority voting; BERTScore for generation
models_tools: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-o3, Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro, Grok 3, Claude Opus, DeepSeek v3, Llama 4 Maverick, Falcon Arabic, Falcon 3, Fanar, ALLaM
main_findings: MCQ: majority vote 77%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 76%, Gemini Flash 74%, GPT-o3 74%, Llama 4 Maverick 63%, GPT-4o 57%, Claude Opus 49%, ALLaM 39%, Falcon Arabic 38%, Falcon 3 36%, Fanar 31%; open-ended BERTScore about 0.84-0.86 for top models (non-discriminating)
limitations: Small dataset; weak metric; prompt sensitivity; manual web testing of Falcon Arabic
relevance: Q2; P4: metric weakness for Arabic generation
supports_or_contradicts: Local Arabic models underperform frontier models; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Arabic-centric models scored 31-39% on AraHealthQA MCQs

title: Bridging Language Barriers in Healthcare: A Study on Arabic LLMs
authors: Nada Saadi, Tathagata Raha, Clement Christophe, Marco AF Pimentel, Ronnie Rajan, Praveen K Kanithi
venue: arXiv 2501.09825 (AAAI 2025 copyright line; venue not confirmed)
objective: Measure Arabic-English medical gap, translation pipelines and Arabic/English fine-tuning mixtures
architecture_methods: Translated MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, MMLU; translate-then-answer; fine-tuning with language mixtures (469.97M tokens)
models_tools: Qwen2.5 3B/7B/72B, Llama 3.1 8B/70B, Mistral-7B, Pangea-7B, Silma-9B, Med42-Llama3.1-70B, Meditron3-70B, BiMedix
main_findings: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MedQA 62.0 En vs 29.5 Ar; Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct 78.2 vs 56.6; Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct Arabic MedQA 76.1; LLM translators 70.5-71.3 vs MT models 31.2-40.8; Arabic-only fine-tuning 8B-Instruct Arabic MMLU 46.4 to 30.0; 70B base Arabic PubMedQA 51.8 to 76.8
limitations: MCQ only; translated benchmarks; template issues; mainly Llama 3.1
relevance: Q2; P1/RQ3 language robustness
supports_or_contradicts: Translation and fine-tuning do not reliably close gap; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Large Arabic-English gap for smaller models

title: Calibration and Conformal Prediction for Medical Question Answering in Arabic and English: Evidence from Two Non-Parallel Benchmarks
authors: Mariya
objective: Compare calibration, conformal sets and selective prediction in Arabic vs English medical MCQ
architecture_methods: Temperature scaling; split conformal prediction at 90% coverage; selective risk
metrics: Accuracy, AUROC, ECE, coverage, set size, selective risk
baselines: English vs Arabic; raw vs temperature-scaled
main_findings: Qwen accuracy 0.561 En vs 0.430 Ar; raw ECE 0.386 vs 0.486, after scaling 0.068 vs 0.035; singleton conformal sets 23.4% En vs 4.9% Ar; top-20% selective risk 0.098 En vs 0.354 Ar; Jais 0.369 vs 0.308 accuracy, strong option-C bias
limitations: Non-GCC single author; non-parallel benchmarks confound language and dataset; two 7B models; no fluent Arabic check; not clinical validation
relevance: P2, RQ1: uncertainty and abstention evidence in Arabic
supports_or_contradicts: Suggests confidence-based abstention less useful in Arabic; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Arabic medical MCQ shows worse calibration and less informative uncertainty sets (confounded)

title: Effectiveness of Informed AI Use on Clinical Competence of General Practitioners and Internists: Pre-Post Intervention Study
authors: Eyad A Qunaibi, Ayman M Al-Qaaneh, Baraa F Ismail, Hussam I Muhidat, Farhia S Rageh, Najwa A Musallam, Alaa K Fawzy
objective: Test whether brief AI-use training plus GPT-4 access improves physicians' case-based test performance
architecture_methods: Quasi-experimental pre-post, alternating test sets, 1.5 h online course
dataset_sample: 326 physicians (229 GPs, 97 internists), 39 countries; co-authors in Qatar and UAE (not GCC-specific)
metrics: Test score, pass rate (80%), time, perceptions
main_findings: Mean score 56.88% to 77.56% (P<.001); pass rate 6.4% (21/326) to 58.6% (191/326); time 40.25 to 42.29 min (P=.03); gains in diagnosis, treatment planning and counselling; GPs gained more than internists (23.7% vs 13.7%)
limitations: No control arm (training and AI access confounded); self-selection; heavy attrition (1,339/1,665); MCQ vignettes; single LLM; author-developed course
relevance: RQ1/P4: human+LLM performance; weak design
supports_or_contradicts: Suggests physician+LLM gains but cannot isolate effect; neutral on multi-agent
claims_supported: Physicians with GPT-4 access after brief training scored higher on case MCQs (uncontrolled)

title: Guidance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies based Medical Devices (MDS-G010)
authors: Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA)

metadata_verified_via: Official SFDA EN and AR pages and PDF
objective: Requirements for AI/ML-based medical devices in KSA
main_findings: Scope: AI/ML that diagnose, manage or predict diseases by analysing medical data; intended use determines device status (MDS-REQ 1 Annex 5); clinical evaluation in 3 stages; local validation for foreign-approved devices; subgroup analysis; clinician with/without comparison; human oversight as operational risk control; evaluate trust, learning curve, automation bias; change notification via GHAD within 10 (significant) or 30 days; PMS and data drift; ISO 13485/14971; no generative AI or CDS-specific provisions

claims_supported: MDS-G010 remains v1.0 and lacks generative-AI provisions
